segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In English, we have many ways to talk about the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you get any random verb like "to eat", for example,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you can say "I ate",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you can say "I have eaten",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you can say "I was eating",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you can say "I used to eat",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: you can say "I would eat an ice cream every week when I was a child",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and they use "would" to speak about the past in English:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I would go to the cinema every day when I was young."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have many different ways of talking about the past, but we can divide them into three,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and in Spanish they are three.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We have the "I have eaten" past,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: which is the one that we learned already: "I have eaten" with haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then the other two pasts, we can think of as a line in the past and a dot in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, what would fit into the line in the past is "I was eating", "I used to eat", "I would eat all the time when I was younger".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: All of that is ongoing, it's like a line in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But then the dot in the past is "I ate"—finished, "I ate", that's your dot in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Those are what we will consider our three different pasts, which all of the different ways of expressing the past in English fit into,

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: and in Spanish we have these three forms.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The one we learned already is "I have eaten", for example.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: First we need to manage the verb "to have".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What is the verb for "to have" in this context?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Haber, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have haber, and we had a neat trick to find the different versions of haber, as we know it's very irregular. So what is "I have"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, and "we have"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And what is "he, she, it, you" formal have or has?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ha.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And "you" informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Has.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And "they have" or "you guys have"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Han.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So that's our panorama of haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And then we need to find "eaten".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, the version after haber—we want to think of it in this way, the version of the verb that comes after haber, rather than trying to translate "eaten",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: because the version of the verb that comes after "have" in English is often so different:

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "I have wanted", "I have been"—very different.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But in Spanish, for -ar verbs we take off -ar and put -ado, and for -er/-ir verbs we take off the -er or -ir and we put -ido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "I have eaten"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He comerido... sorry, comido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. You're taking off your ending and putting -ido. The only times we're adding on to the "to" forms is with the futures, will and would.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He comido. "I have spoken"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He hablado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He hablado, good. "I have danced"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He bailado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "They have danced"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Han bailado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Han bailado. The version that comes after haber—comido, bailado—it doesn't change for "I" or for "we" or for "they" or for "he" or "she", always the same.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We need to focus on haber, to get the correct version of haber, and then we have the version of the verb that comes afterwards, so: he bailado, han bailado, hemos bailado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can also say more complicated things like "I have been able to eat".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What is "to be able", related to "power"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Poder.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Poder, good. So, "I have been able"—the version that comes after haber, rather than translating "been able", we just want poder after haber. So let's do that first. "I have been able"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He podido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To eat"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. He podido comer. "I have been able to eat." "I haven't been able to eat"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No he podido comer.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No he podido comer. So we can make more interesting structures as well like this using haber.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We can also put haber in "would" time, which gives us the opportunity to make some useful structures. What is our sound for "would"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: -ía.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, "I would have" from haber?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habería... habría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, the 'e' fell out: habría. What was "to leave" or "to go out"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Salir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salir. So you can say "I would have gone out". "I would have gone out"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: He saldría?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you've taken the... the sentence as a block to translate it all together, and then you've had this kind of salad situation where... where this -ía is coming out in the wrong place. You must... you must take the time to divide it up. "I would have" is your first bit and you stop there, ah? "I would have", what's that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habería... habría.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habría. Good, and it's a very natural irregularity. You can imagine many years of saying habería, habería, habería, habería, habería, it happens very naturally for that 'e' to fall out. Only happens with a few verbs, though: habría. So, "I would have gone out"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habría salido.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habría salido, good. "I would have been able to go out"? "I would have been able to go out"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Habría podido salir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Habría podido salir. "I wouldn't have been able to go out"? "I wouldn't have been able to go out"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No habría podido salir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No habría podido salir, good. So we have this haber that we can use for the past, but then also we can make some other very useful structures out of it like "would have", "would have been able", etc.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So now we're going to focus on another past in Spanish. We're going to focus now on the line in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the line in the past representing "I was eating", "I used to eat", "I would eat all the time"—that "would" that we use for past—all of those are represented by this line in the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now for the pasts, for both pasts—the line and the point—again we are taking off our verb ending before we add on our endings for the past.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have a verb like hablar, for example, an -ar verb, and we will take off this -ar and we will put -aba, -aba, to get "I, he, she, it, you" formal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So again, like in "would" time, we have "I" jumping in with "he, she, it" and "you" formal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, you have hablar, you take off the -ar and you put -aba?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaba. Hablaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So hablaba means "I was speaking", "I used to speak", "he was speaking", "she was speaking", "he used to speak", "she used to speak", "you were speaking", "you used to speak"—all of this in hablaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now you can probably make the other versions. How would you say "you were speaking", speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablabas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And "they" or "you guys were speaking"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablaban.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaban.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And for the "we" version, the accent is going to stay in the same place, on -aba. So how would you say "we were speaking"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablábamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablábamos, good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To wait" is esperar. Esperar. To wait or to hope.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "I was waiting", "I used to wait"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Esperaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "I was waiting for you", speaking informally, and we don't need the "for", no? "I was awaiting you."

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Te esperaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Te esperaba. What if you were speaking formally, if you were speaking to usted and you wanted to say "I was waiting for you"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Is it lo?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo esperaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Or to a female it would be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La esperaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So lo and la, other than "it" and "him" and "she", can also mean "you" formal. We see those are always pairing together: he, she, it and you formal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Keeping it formal, speaking to usted, how would you say "we were waiting for you"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo esperábamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo esperábamos, very good. And what if you wanted to say "we were waiting for you guys"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los esperábamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los esperábamos. And of course this could also mean "we were waiting for them", los esperábamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To try", related to "intent"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intentar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, intentar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "I was trying"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intentaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good, intentaba. "He was trying"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intentaba.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. What was "to find", "to encounter"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Encontrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say "they were trying to find it"? "They were trying to find it". So divide up the thoughts: "they were trying", the first bit?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intentaba... intentaban.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Encontrarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Intentaban encontrarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you wanted to say "they were trying to find it for me", the most natural way of saying this in Spanish is "they were trying to find me it", "they were trying to find me it"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intentaban encontrármelo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Intentaban encontrármelo. Good. "They were trying to find me it."

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if you wanted to emphasize "they were trying to find me it", then you could say this sentence in the way that we would probably say it in English, which is "they were trying to find it for me". Then you could do that in Spanish, you have that option. So how would you say that: "they were trying to find it for me", using the word "for"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Intentaban encontrarlo para mí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Intentaban encontrarlo para mí. So here we are emphasizing actually "me". But mostly in Spanish we kind of avoid the use of the preposition, as we've been noticing: intentaban encontrármelo.
